name: Otoro
confidence_why: Stevenson's grammar (2009, a 1943 typescript, relayed by Tucker and Bryan 1966 and by Quint 2010) reports dynamic stress in Otoro with no established pattern, often final and especially before a final consonant but initial in many disyllables, while Quint 2010 and Quint 2020 hold that Otoro is probably a tone language and Stevenson's phonology unreliable, so neither the type of system nor any placement rule is settled.

catalog_quote: [Quint 2010: 311-312, reviewing Stevenson 2009] First, Stevenson completely failed (or refused?) to give comprehensive tone rules for TI and OT, stating that each one of these two languages “is not a tone language in the fullest sense of the term” (p. 17 for TI; 141 for OT), while all recent works devoted to Heibanian languages (Quint 2009: 129-148; Jenks & Rose 2011: 3f; Schadeberg 1981a: 61, 65, 69 etc.) seem to show that most of them (including probably TI and OT) are tone languages. [English Wikipedia 'Otoro language', §Stress and Intonation, citing Stevenson 2009: 141] Stress and the emphasis of louder or stronger sounds are commonly used in the Otoro language. However, words which are only determined by tone are rare. A distinct pattern of the stress in this language has not yet been established, although Stevenson says that the stress often falls on the last syllable. In instance, where a word has a final consonant, the stress typically occurs on the last syllable. Conversely, many dissyllabic words tend to stress on the first syllable. [table cited to Stevenson 2009: 142, 'stress syllable marked ' ', Kwara / Kwijur / Orombe] buttock 'gwutu / 'gwuthu / 'gwutu; many gwu'tu / gwu'tu / gwu'tu; to open 'iðu / 'iðu / 'iðhu; head l'ɽa / l'ɽa / l'ɽa

new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand only. Stevenson (1943 ms., publ. 2009: 141-142) treats Otoro as a stress language ('not a tone language in the fullest sense'), with no fixed stress position: stress is reported as often final (especially in consonant-final words) but initial in many disyllables, and stress position can distinguish words (Kwara 'gwutu 'buttock' vs gwu'tu 'many', p.142 per Wikipedia) — i.e. lexical/unpredictable stress on his analysis. Modern Heiban specialists (Schadeberg 1981a; Quint 2010, 2020) instead regard Otoro as a two-level tone language, implying Stevenson's 'stress' marks largely reflect tone. Hence unclear/contradictory pending the primary pages.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing reported in the sources opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Per the Wikipedia paraphrase of Stevenson: consonant-final words tend to final stress; many disyllables initial stress; minimal pairs by stress position exist.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms (Stevenson's stress-marked vocabulary, Kwara dialect with Kwijur/Orombe variants). The stress-location wording comes from a tertiary source (Wikipedia) paraphrasing Stevenson 2009:141-142; the verbatim review quote (Quint) concerns the tone-vs-stress status, not the position. No first-hand page was opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Stevenson's grammar (1943 ms., publ. 2009) describes the Kwara dialect of Otoro, with supplementary notes on the Kwijur and Orombe dialects (per Jakobi 2013 and Quint 2010); all fall under Glottolog otor1240 (Otoro; alt. names Utoro, Dhitoro, Litoro, Kawama/Kawarma). Modern Heiban specialists (Schadeberg 1981; Quint 2010, 2020) analyse Heiban languages, probably including Otoro, as two-level tone languages, so Stevenson's 'stress' marking may partly encode tone.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing statement (Quint 2010 reporting Stevenson 2009: 141, Otoro 'is not a tone language in the fullest sense of the term'): both describe a stress-plus-tone system in which stress outranks pitch. Tucker & Bryan add that Stevenson (1956-57 data) ranks dynamic stress above syllabic pitch for the whole Koalib-Moro/Talodi-Masakin/Lafofa group, but give no stress-placement rule and no Otoro-specific example, so the catalog's empty rule field stays empty. The statement is group-level (K-M/T-M/L), not Otoro-specific.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Koalib-Moro (incl. Otoro), Talodi-Masakin and Lafofa languages as a group, Tucker & Bryan quote Stevenson: dynamic stress, carried together with a High or Low tone, matters more than pitch as such, but its prominence differs from language to language; the importance of tone is not yet investigated and only a few lexical tone doublets (from Laro and Masakin, none from Otoro) are cited. No placement rule for stress is given, and the examples are left unmarked for tone and stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the only qualification is that stress 'is not equally prominent in all languages' of the group.
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's statement covers the Koalib-Moro (Heiban) group together with Talodi-Masakin and Lafofa; Otoro is named in the chapter's noun-class and verb tables but the stress sentence is group-level and is Stevenson's own wording (Stevenson 1956-57, Afrika und Übersee 40-41). Tone examples come from Laro (K-M) and Masakin (T-M), not Otoro.
